clue.text: Stop copper, a good sort

parts.note: Cu is the chemical symbol for copper
a toff is a smart, well-dressed person, in old slang a fine fellow

explanation.surface: Someone tells a decent police officer to halt.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Copper' reads as a policeman, but it is the metal. A toff is British slang for a posh, upper-class person.
explanation.definitionFit: To cut off a supply or a speaker is to stop it abruptly, so the phrasal verb matches.

clue.text: Generous daily, albeit misguidedly

parts.note: a daily, or char, is a cleaning lady who comes in each day

indicators.note: something done misguidedly goes astray, so the word before it is scrambled out of its order

parts.note: taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A newspaper is praised as generous, though the praise is misplaced.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Daily' looks like a newspaper, but in British usage it is also a daily help, a cleaner, also called a char.
explanation.definitionFit: Charitable means kindly and giving freely, which is a straightforward synonym for generous.

clue.text: Pleasant to touch, climbing cat I let out

indicators.note: in a down clue climbing means reading upwards, so the word is turned back to front

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: out suggests letters thrown out of place, so the preceding words are scrambled

parts.note: taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A soft cat that climbs is nice to stroke, so the owner lets it outdoors.
explanation.definitionFit: Tactile is used of fabrics and surfaces that feel pleasing to the hand, a common modern sense.

clue.text: Fine island bird

parts.note: F is the abbreviation for fine, as on pencil leads
an inch is a small island, a Scottish word found in place names like Inchcolm

explanation.surface: A splendid bird found on an island.
explanation.walkthrough: Inch for island is a Scottish usage seen in many place names.
explanation.definitionFit: A finch is a small seed-eating songbird, so it is an example of a bird.

clue.text: Alarm! Oil running out, here in Texas

indicators.note: running out suggests things spilling loose and disordered, so the preceding letters are jumbled

parts.note: taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Panic in a Texan oil town as the wells run dry.
explanation.definitionFit: Amarillo is a city in the Texas Panhandle, so it is a place that could be called here in Texas.

clue.text: Drink fizzy wine and rare malt

indicators.note: fizzy suggests bubbling agitation, so the words that follow are stirred into a new order

parts.note: taken as written, to be rearranged
taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A drinks order: sparkling wine and a rare single malt whisky.
explanation.definitionFit: Mineral water is bottled spring water, often sparkling, so it is a kind of drink.

clue.text: Mean about gift

parts.note: re means concerning or about
a present is a gift

explanation.surface: Someone stingy grumbles over a gift.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mean' looks like stingy, but it is the verb: to signify.
explanation.definitionFit: To represent something is to stand for or signify it, which is what a symbol means.

clue.text: I suffer over boy's affair

indicators.note: over means turned over, so the preceding words are read in the opposite direction

parts.note: taken as written
to ail is to suffer or be unwell
a son is a boy

explanation.surface: A parent laments a son's romantic entanglement.
explanation.definitionFit: A liaison is a secret sexual relationship, so it is a synonym for an affair.

clue.text: Frank, old writer

parts.note: O is the abbreviation for old
a pen is an instrument for writing

explanation.surface: A man named Frank who was once an author.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Frank' looks like a name, but it is the adjective meaning candid.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone open speaks candidly and hides nothing, which is a synonym for frank.

clue.text: Mysterious, first half of Cats penned by composer

indicators.note: something penned by another is shut inside it, as in a pen or enclosure

parts.note: Thomas Arne, English composer of Rule, Britannia

indicators.note: first half of tells us to keep only the opening portion of the next word

parts.note: the first two of its four letters

explanation.surface: Something obscure about the musical Cats written by a composer.
explanation.walkthrough: Arne is a crossword regular: the 18th-century composer of Rule, Britannia.
explanation.definitionFit: Arcane means understood only by a few, secret or obscure, a direct synonym for mysterious.

clue.text: Note a pal changed with no effort

indicators.note: changed tells us the letters before it are altered into a different arrangement

parts.note: taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A lazy friend's note was altered without any trouble.
explanation.definitionFit: Handed something on a plate means getting it without having to work for it, an idiom for effortlessly.

clue.text: Withdraw, exhausted, to a sanctuary

parts.note: beat means worn out, tired
taken as written
a retreat is a quiet refuge

explanation.surface: A tired person withdraws to a peaceful sanctuary.
explanation.definitionFit: To beat a retreat is an idiom from military drumming meaning to pull back or leave hastily.

clue.text: Girl volunteers to cage first of hound dogs

indicators.note: to cage something is to enclose it, so one piece sits inside the others

parts.note: Iris is a girl's name
Terriers is a nickname for members of the Territorial Army, Britain's volunteer reserve

indicators.note: first of tells us to keep only the initial letter of the next word

parts.note: the opening letter

explanation.surface: A girl's volunteer helpers pen up a hound among the dogs.
explanation.walkthrough: The Territorial Army is Britain's part-time volunteer reserve; its soldiers are nicknamed Terriers. The H sits in the join between the two words.
explanation.definitionFit: Irish terriers are a breed of red-coated terrier, so they are examples of dogs.

clue.text: Where teachers may be, in form fatso's vandalised

indicators.note: vandalised things are smashed up, so the preceding letters are broken and reassembled

parts.note: taken as written, the possessive s included, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Teachers gather after a pupil in their class has trashed their space.
explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe s counts as a letter of the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Staff rooms are the lounges in schools set aside for teachers, so they are places teachers may be found.

clue.text: Article located in ruins? That's hearsay

definitions.note: used adjectivally, as in hearsay evidence

parts.note: an is the indefinite article

indicators.note: something in ruins has collapsed into disorder, so the word before it is rebuilt differently

parts.note: taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A report claims some object was found among ruins, but it's only rumour.
explanation.definitionFit: Anecdotal evidence rests on stories passed on rather than proof, the same quality as hearsay.

clue.text: Flirting, daughter before marriage

parts.note: d is the abbreviation for daughter
an alliance can be a union by marriage

explanation.surface: A daughter flirts before she is married.
explanation.definitionFit: Dalliance is casual romantic play or trifling, which is a noun matching flirting.

clue.text: Painter from eastern state

indicators.note: from signals the letters are taken out of the run of words that follows

parts.note: letters running across the two words

explanation.surface: An artist who comes from an eastern state.
explanation.walkthrough: Max Ernst was a German Surrealist painter.
explanation.definitionFit: Max Ernst was a leading Dada and Surrealist artist, so he is an example of a painter.

clue.text: Colonel knocked back a litre in nearby pub

indicators.note: knocked back means sent backwards, so the word before it is read in reverse

parts.note: Col is the abbreviation for colonel
taken as written
l is the abbreviation for litre

explanation.surface: An army officer downs a litre of beer at the pub round the corner.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Knocked back' suggests drinking, but it signals turning the colonel back to front. In Britain your local is your neighbourhood pub.
explanation.definitionFit: The local is a British term for the pub nearest one's home that one regularly visits.

clue.text: Female creature's sitting on border flower

parts.note: a cow is a female animal, with the possessive s
a lip is an edge or rim

explanation.surface: A cow is sitting on the edge of a flowerbed.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue, sitting on puts the first piece above the second. 'Border' suggests a garden bed, but it is just an edge.
explanation.definitionFit: The cowslip is a yellow wild primula of meadows, so it is a kind of flower.

clue.text: This could be best fare (including duck)

definitions.text: This could be best fare (including duck)

indicators.note: could be suggests the letters might become something else once rearranged

parts.note: taken as written, to be rearranged
a duck in cricket is a score of nought, shaped like O

explanation.surface: A menu note says the best dish, with duck added, is this one.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue does both jobs: roast beef is the classic best Sunday fare. Including adds the O to the letters before they are shuffled.
explanation.definitionFit: Roast beef is Britain's traditional Sunday dinner, so it could well be called the best fare.

clue.text: Yachtswoman Tracy saw red, drifting round close to dockyard

indicators.note: round means surrounding, so the scrambled letters go about the other piece
drifting things wander loosely off course, so these letters move out of order

parts.note: taken as written, to be rearranged

indicators.note: close to means the end of, so only the final letter of the next word is kept

parts.note: the final letter

explanation.surface: A sailor lost her temper while drifting near the docks.
explanation.walkthrough: Tracy Edwards skippered Maiden, the first all-female crew in the Whitbread Round the World Race.
explanation.definitionFit: Tracy Edwards is a British sailor who led the first all-female crew round the world, so she is the yachtswoman named.

clue.text: One who exposes referee?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: someone who reveals wrongdoing inside an organisation
second meaning, taken literally: an official who sounds a whistle

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags that the second meaning is a playful literal reading of the compound.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means an insider who reveals misconduct, and read literally describes a match official who sounds the whistle.

clue.text: Doctor about to inject into raised part of foot

indicators.note: in a down clue raised means read upwards, so the word is turned around
to inject is to put something inside, so one piece goes within the other

parts.note: the heel is the back part of the foot
c, for circa, means about

explanation.surface: A doctor is about to give an injection in a patient's raised foot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Doctor' looks like the wordplay's instruction, but it is the definition, in an old sense.
explanation.definitionFit: Leech is an archaic word for a physician, from the bloodsucking worms doctors once applied.

clue.text: Minister's short skirt

indicators.note: short means cut off before the end, so the final letters of the word before it are dropped

parts.note: taken as written, before trimming

explanation.surface: A government minister wears a daring short skirt.
explanation.walkthrough: The source text reads 'Sister's', which gives nothing; the clue only works as 'Minister's', with the minister cut short. The 's links the wordplay to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A mini is the common short name for a miniskirt, a skirt ending well above the knee.

clue.text: I tell lies about one from Jersey, perhaps

parts.note: taken as written
to slander is to spread false, damaging statements about someone

explanation.surface: Someone confesses to telling lies about a Jersey resident.
explanation.walkthrough: Jersey is a Channel Island, so the 'perhaps' marks a native as one example.
explanation.definitionFit: Jersey is an island, so someone from there is an example of an islander.

clue.text: I rowed angrily with a strange person

indicators.note: doing something angrily implies agitation, so the words before it are thrown into a new order

parts.note: taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone admits to quarrelling furiously with an odd stranger.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rowed' reads as rowing a boat, but here it rhymes with 'loud': quarrelled.
explanation.definitionFit: Weirdo is an informal noun for someone eccentric or odd, a synonym for a strange person.

clue.text: Ninety, possibly, round centre of Naples, and teeming

indicators.note: round means surrounding, so the rearranged letters wrap the other piece
possibly hints the word may be read another way, so its letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written, to be rearranged

indicators.note: centre of tells us to keep only the middle letters of the next word

parts.note: the middle two of its six letters

explanation.surface: Ninety-odd people crowd round the heart of Naples, which is packed.
explanation.definitionFit: Things in plenty exist in large numbers, so the phrase means abundant, teeming.

clue.text: Paper is written after the end of Michaelmas

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: end of tells us to keep only the final letter of the next word

parts.note: the final letter
taken as written

explanation.surface: A student's essay is due at the close of the Michaelmas term.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The' reads as part of 'the end of', but it is taken literally as the opening letters; Michaelmas is the autumn term at Oxford and Cambridge.
explanation.definitionFit: A thesis is a long academic dissertation, and paper is a common word for such a written study.
